coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development

evidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.

coursesExamined.name: Modern History

Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.

coursesExamined.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy

evidence.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
evidence.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
evidence.discipline: Ancient history; Archaeology; Classical studies; Political sociology
evidence.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
evidence.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design

descriptions.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
descriptions.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.

descriptions.text: Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.

sharedReview.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

qualitativeDistinctness: Culture is organised around identity, representation and power through a sustained sequence of gender history, empire, heritage, social movements, political philosophy and conflict, alongside direct art, literary and media analysis. It differs from the preceding alternatives by [9] courses respectively; these differences follow the concepts and are not arbitrary threshold substitutions.

The programme shifts emphasis from broad visual-art and social-theory study to literary interpretation, adaptation, documentary and a 30-EC rhetoric, stylistics, persuasion and creative-communication sequence. Archaeology and philosophy supply specific complementary analytical contexts. It differs from the preceding alternatives by [5, 12] courses respectively; these differences follow the concepts and are not arbitrary threshold substitutions.
comparability: All three materially address arts and cultural interpretation, not coherence through generic humanities alone. Objects/media, theories and methods have sustained weight. Broad repertoire vs identity/power vs literature/film/communication priorities drive real 9/5/12-course differences. No superficial numerical substitutions. Political/history/ethics and public communication contributions remain specific complementary contexts, not substitutes for arts.

stopping.assessment: Three provisional concepts remain supported by exact-target interests and actual UCR content: broad arts/media/cultural analysis; culture, identity and power; literature, film and communication. Three institutional-politics courses in the second route are replaced with art history, stylistics and film adaptation to give cultural objects adequate weight. Performance/music/festival interests remain evidenced but cannot produce an additional included route under the three-alternative maximum, and UCR lacks the dedicated music and performing-arts sequence. These concepts respond to the defining arts-and-cultural-interpretation substance of the official indicative 2027 intake pathway; specialist music, performance, festival and thesis gaps remain explicit.

alignment: Both introduce close visual analysis and interpretation of artworks in historical context.

Partial theoretical correspondence: art historiography examines aesthetics, meaning and interpretation within the history of art history; it does not reproduce a dedicated philosophical aesthetics course.

Partial correspondence through feminist, Marxist and cultural-minority readings of literature. UCR examines how interpretive perspectives shape meaning, rather than reproducing the whole Literature and Power course.

Partial contextual correspondence: European and wider political, social and economic history from 1815 onward; not the comparator’s full cultural repertoire or global-period coverage.

Planetary Culture is a dedicated 10-EC component. UCR environmental-media courses address representations and ecological questions, but the available evidence does not establish the same primary scope for one counterpart.
Both develop academic argument, source use, writing and oral presentation; UCR uses rhetoric as its organising framework.

Partial methodological correspondence: UCR teaches qualitative design, data collection and interpretation. Radboud requires research methods specifically for cultural studies; identical method coverage is not asserted.
Dedicated art criticism. UCR develops interpretation and argument in several courses but has no single scheduled professional arts-review course.
A required festival-production course. UCR creative communication develops poetic and hybrid projects, with no guaranteed festival or cultural-sector placement.
